note_text: Aristarchus of Samos proposed his heliocentric model in the 3rd century BC (c. 280–270 BC), not the 2nd century. Historical records place his life between approximately 310 and 230 BC. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristarchus_of_Samos https://www.britannica.com/biography/Aristarchus-of-Samos
claim: Aristarchus proposed heliocentrism in the second century BC.
context: Maybe the clearest example is Aristarchus in the second century BC comes up with the idea of heliocentrism. The ancient Athenians dismiss it on the grounds that we should see as the Earth is moving around the Sun, if really the Sun is the center of the solar system, the stars move relative to the Earth.

source_verification.reasoning: Both sources confirm Aristarchus lived c. 310–230 BC (3rd century BC). Wikipedia confirms his solstice observation in 280 BC and explicitly states the heliocentric system was proposed during the third century BC, supporting the c. 280–270 BC claim. All factual claims in the note are covered.

citations.quote: **Aristarchus of Samos** (; [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀρίσταρχος ὁ Σάμιος, _Aristarkhos ho Samios_; c. 310 – c. 230 BC) was an [ancient Greek astronomer](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_astronomy "Ancient Greek astronomy")
citations.explanation: Confirms life span c. 310–230 BC, supporting the note's date range.

citations.quote: According to Ptolemy, Aristarchus observed the [summer solstice](/wiki/Summer_solstice "Summer solstice") of 280 BC.
citations.explanation: Supports that his activity was in the early 3rd century BC, consistent with c. 280–270 BC for his model.

citations.quote: The Greek mathematician and astronomer Aristarchus of Samos proposed such a system during the third century BC
citations.explanation: Directly supports the claim that the heliocentric model was 3rd century BC, not 2nd.

citations.quote: **Aristarchus of Samos** (born _c._ 310 bce—died _c._ 230 bce) was a Greek astronomer who maintained that [Earth](http://web.archive.org/web/20260425091815/https://www.britannica.com/place/Earth) rotates on its axis and revolves around the [Sun](http://web.archive.org/web/20260425091815/https://www.britannica.com/place/Sun).
citations.explanation: Confirms birth and death dates c. 310–230 BC, supporting the note's stated range.
